title: Knowing Others Have Minds
objective: After this level you can explain theory of mind and the false-belief test used to show when children develop it.
summary: Theory of mind is understanding that others can think and believe differently from you. False-belief tests like the Sally-Anne task show it arrives around age 4 to 5, at a similar age across cultures.

cards.headline: Anne moves Sally's marble while Sally is away. Where will Sally look?
cards.body: You know the marble moved. Sally doesn't. Getting the answer right means holding two versions of the world in mind: what is true, and what Sally believes. Young children often get it wrong, and the age when they start getting it right tells psychologists something big.

cards.headline: Minds that differ from yours
cards.body: Theory of mind is understanding that other people have thoughts, feelings and beliefs different from your own. Children develop it between about 3 and 5 years old. Psychologists usually spot it with false-belief tasks, which test whether a child understands that someone else can believe something that isn't true. You can't see a belief, so the test has to make one visible.

cards.headline: The Sally-Anne task
cards.body: In one classic false-belief test, a child watches a short scene. Sally puts her marble away and leaves. While she's gone, Anne moves the marble into her own box. Then comes the key question: where will Sally look for her marble? Past the age of 4 to 5, most children say Sally will look where she left it. In early studies, younger children systematically got it wrong, as if Sally must know what they know.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: passing isn't about knowing where the marble is. It's knowing that Sally doesn't.

cards.headline: Same milestone, many cultures
cards.body: Is this a quirk of Western children? In 2005, Tara Callaghan and colleagues gave one standard false-belief test to children in Canada, India, Peru, Samoa and Thailand. In every culture, children passed at about age 5. A 2001 review of 178 studies, led by Henry Wellman, found the same shift across countries: preschoolers go from below-chance to above-chance on false-belief tasks.

learned: Theory of mind develops around ages 3 to 5

questions.prompt: Match each idea or study of theory of mind with its description.

pairs.right: Canada, India, Peru, Samoa and Thailand

questions.explanation: Children develop theory of mind between about 3 and 5 years old. Callaghan's team tested children in Canada, India, Peru, Samoa and Thailand, and Henry Wellman led a review of 178 studies.

questions.prompt: In the Sally-Anne task, a child who understands false belief answers that Sally will _____.

options.label: look where she left the marble
look where Anne put the marble
options.rationale: That's where it really is, but Sally didn't see it move.

options.label: know the marble moved
options.rationale: Sally was away when it moved.

options.label: stop looking for the marble
options.rationale: The task asks where she will look.

questions.explanation: Sally still believes the marble is where she left it; a child who says so understands that Sally holds a false belief.

questions.prompt: Cognitive science treats the mind as holding representations. What must a child track to pass the Sally-Anne task?

options.label: Only where the marble really is now
options.rationale: That leads to the wrong answer.

options.label: How many times Anne moved the marble from one hiding place to another
options.rationale: Counting moves doesn't reveal what Sally believes.

options.label: Which doll is taller
options.rationale: Size has nothing to do with the task.

options.label: Sally's belief, a representation that no longer matches reality

questions.explanation: Passing means keeping in mind Sally's own picture of the world, which is now out of date.
